Probability of Superiority for a Paired-Samples Design

Source: R/probability_of_superiority_paired.R
probability_of_superiority_paired.Rd

Takes paired observations and returns the probability of superiority for a paired design (Grissom & Kim, 2005, 2012), the probability that the second member of a pair scores higher than the first (a tied pair counting one half), with a confidence interval and the numbers of pairs won, lost, and tied. Only the order within each pair is used. It is the paired counterpart of vargha_delaney_A and cliff_delta, which are for two independent groups.

Usage

probability_of_superiority_paired(x, y, conf_level = 0.95)

Arguments

x, y

Paired numeric vectors of equal length. \(x\) and \(y\) are interpreted as repeated measurements on the same units (e.g., pre/post, condition 1 / condition 2, sibling-1 / sibling-2). Logical vectors and ordered factors with the same levels in the same order are also accepted, since only the order within each pair is used. Pairs with a missing member are removed (see the n_missing attribute). An unordered factor and a character vector are refused; see What is refused, and why.

conf_level

Confidence level. Default 0.95.

Value

A data.frame (classes dmar_probability_of_superiority_paired and dmar_tbl) with columns term and value and these rows:

probability_of_superiority

The estimate \(\hat P_S\), the proportion of pairs with \(y_i > x_i\) plus half the proportion of tied pairs.

ci_lower, ci_upper

The confidence limits at conf_level. Both equal the estimate when the estimated variance is 0, and are then not a confidence interval.

var_ps

The estimated variance of \(\hat P_S\).

wins_y_over_x

The number of complete pairs with \(y_i > x_i\).

losses_y_under_x

The number with \(y_i < x_i\).

ties

The number with \(y_i = x_i\).

The table carries the attributes conf_level; n_missing, the number of pairs removed because a member was missing; and interval_degenerate, present only when the estimated variance is 0, with the value "complete_separation" or "no_variation". The tidy() and glance() verbs (see dmar_tidiers) add a logical column interval_degenerate.

Details

Estimand and interval. For a pair \((X, Y)\) drawn from the population of pairs, $$P_S \;=\; \Pr(Y > X) + 0.5 \cdot \Pr(Y = X).$$ The sampling unit is the pair, and the \(n\) pairs are taken to be independent and identically distributed; nothing is assumed about the distribution of the scores or about the dependence within a pair. The interval is a large-sample confidence interval for \(P_S\), formed on a transformed scale that keeps it inside \([0, 1]\). A value of 0.5 says that neither member tends to score higher.

Sample estimate. With the score of pair \(i\) $$s_i = \mathrm{I}(y_i > x_i) + 0.5 \cdot \mathrm{I}(y_i = x_i),$$ the estimate is the mean \(\hat P_S = \bar s\): the proportion of pairs won by \(y\), plus half the proportion tied. Being the mean of \(n\) independent scores with expectation \(P_S\), it is unbiased. Each pair is compared directly, not through the difference \(y_i - x_i\), so a pair of equal infinite values is a tie.

Why a function for pairs. \(P_S\) compares the two members of one pair. Vargha and Delaney's A and Cliff's \(\delta\) compare an observation of one group with an observation of an unrelated unit in the other, which is a different quantity when the members of a pair are correlated, and the variance formulas of vargha_delaney_A and cliff_delta assume independent groups. Paired data therefore need the estimate and the variance given here.

Variance and confidence interval. The variance of the mean of \(n\) independent scores is the variance of a score divided by \(n\), and the function estimates it by $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat P_S) \;=\; \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (s_i - \bar s)^2,$$ which uses the divisor \(n\) in the variance of the scores (it is \((n - 1)/n\) times the estimate with the divisor \(n - 1\)). This is the row var_ps. The interval is formed for \(d = 2 P_S - 1\), which lies in \([-1, 1]\), on the scale of \(\mathrm{arctanh}(d)\), as the interval of cliff_delta is: $$\tanh\!\left\{\mathrm{arctanh}(\hat d) \pm z_{1 - \alpha/2}\, \frac{2\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat P_S)}}{1 - \hat d^2} \right\},$$ and the two limits \(d_L\) and \(d_U\) are returned as \((d_L + 1)/2\) and \((d_U + 1)/2\).

Scale and missing values. Only the order within each pair is used, so any increasing rescoring applied to both members gives the same result, and an ordinal response may be supplied as two ordered factors with the same levels. A pair with a missing member (NA or NaN) is removed, and the number removed is in the n_missing attribute. x and y must have the same length. Fewer than three complete pairs is an error, since no variance can be estimated.

What is refused, and why. The statistic uses the order of the observations and nothing else, so the function must be given objects whose order is the order meant. It refuses, with a condition of class dmar_scores_not_ordered (see dmar_metadata), an unordered factor (its codes follow the order of levels(), alphabetical unless set, so the levels low, mid, high are stored as 2, 3, 1); a character vector (strings sort alphabetically, "10" before "9"); an ordered factor beside anything that is not an ordered factor with the same levels in the same order (each factor numbers its own levels from 1); time differences in different units, or one beside plain numbers (each such object is stored in its own units); a Date beside a POSIXct; and a list, data frame, or matrix of several columns. Nothing is computed in any of these cases. The message says which case applies and what to supply: an ordered factor with its levels from lowest to highest, factor(x, levels = c("low", "mid", "high"), ordered = TRUE), or numeric scores.

When the estimated variance is zero. Two kinds of data give a variance estimate of exactly 0, and they are the only two. Complete separation: every pair favors the same member, so the estimate is at the end of its range (0 or 1). No variation: every pair is tied, so the estimate is 0.5. In both, the two limits are reported equal to the estimate, var_ps is 0, the table's interval_degenerate attribute names the case, and a warning of class dmar_interval_degenerate is given whose reason element is "complete_separation" or "no_variation"; the condition also carries estimate and n (the number of pairs), and its limit_feng_cliff is NA, since that limit is for two independent groups. The reported limits are not a confidence interval with the stated coverage. The zero describes the sample: the variance estimate measures how much the scores differ from one pair to the next, and when every pair favors the same member they do not differ. Complete separation is common when the effect is large and the pairs are few. Without ties, \(n\) pairs all favor the same member with probability \(P_S^n + (1 - P_S)^n\): 0.47 for five pairs and 0.22 for ten when \(P_S = 0.86\), and 0.82 and 0.66 when \(P_S = 0.96\). In those samples the reported limits, both 0 or both 1, do not contain a population value inside (0, 1).

Particular cases. Infinite values are ordered like any others, and a pair of equal infinite values is a tie. Wins together with ties, and no losses, give a positive variance and an ordinary interval (three wins and a tie give 0.875 with limits 0.502 and 0.980). The mark travels with the result: results_sentence writes the estimate and says that there is no confidence interval, the printed table says so beneath itself, and tidy() and glance() carry it in the column interval_degenerate. The randomization test for paired observations (randomization_test_paired) remains valid in both cases.

Reading the output. In the example below 20 of the 30 pairs have a higher post than pre score and none is tied, so \(\hat P_S = 20/30 = 0.667\), with 95 percent limits 0.484 and 0.810.

References

Grissom, R. J., & Kim, J. J. (2005). Effect sizes for research: A broad practical approach. Lawrence Erlbaum.

Grissom, R. J., & Kim, J. J. (2012). Effect sizes for research: Univariate and multivariate applications (2nd ed.). Routledge.

Vargha, A., & Delaney, H. D. (2000). A critique and improvement of the CL common language effect size statistics of McGraw and Wong. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 25(2), 101–132. doi:10.3102/10769986025002101

See also

Examples

# 1. Paired pre/post data:
set.seed(113)
pre  <- rnorm(30, mean = 100, sd = 15)
post <- pre + rnorm(30, mean =  5, sd = 10)
probability_of_superiority_paired(x = pre, y = post)
#>  term                       value
#>  probability_of_superiority 0.667
#>  ci_lower                   0.484
#>  ci_upper                   0.810
#>  var_ps                     0.007
#>  wins_y_over_x              20   
#>  losses_y_under_x           10   
#>  ties                       0    
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 2. Every pair favors the same member: the estimated variance is 0,
#    the two limits equal the estimate, and a warning says that they
#    are not a confidence interval.
all_up <- probability_of_superiority_paired(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
                                            y = c(4, 5, 6, 7))
#> Warning: probability_of_superiority_paired(): every pair favors the same member (probability of superiority = 1), so the estimated variance is 0. Both confidence limits are reported equal to the estimate (1, 1). They are not a confidence interval with the stated coverage: the variance estimate is built from how much the comparisons differ from one pair to the next, and in a sample in which every pair favors the same member they do not differ at all. That describes this sample, not the population. A population in which some pairs favor the other member often produces a sample with none when there are few pairs (here 4 pairs), so the limits must not be read as showing that the population value is 1. Report the estimate with the sample size and say that every pair favored the same member; the randomization test (randomization_test_paired()) gives a p-value that remains valid here.
all_up
#>  term                       value
#>  probability_of_superiority 1.000
#>  ci_lower                   1.000
#>  ci_upper                   1.000
#>  var_ps                     0.000
#>  wins_y_over_x              4    
#>  losses_y_under_x           0    
#>  ties                       0    
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Limits are not a confidence interval: the estimated variance is 0.
results_sentence(all_up)
#> [1] "probability_of_superiority = 1.00 (no confidence interval: every pair favors the same member, so the estimated variance is 0)"
